High School. American History class. 

I had a teacher like Mr. Wolfson. And without him, I wouldn't have lived the life I have. Then, it was a life I could only imagine.

My teacher was Mr. Armstrong. He was the AP U.S. history teacher. I was the only kid in the class who came from a working class background. The rest of the kids were upper middle class - vacations in Europe each summer, new cars, beautiful homes, tutors for every subject. They had everything I didn't have. But I soon realized this: I might not ever have what they had, but I could know what they knew. 

I was soon one of the best students in the class. How did that happen? A good teacher makes students want to work hard. 

Mr. Armstrong encouraged me, took the time to have real talks with me, about what I would study in college, assuming I could afford college anywhere. In 1971 he told me I should consider being a lawyer. Me. A young ethnic girl from a working class background. But he told me I could do this. And when I got the highest score in his class on the AP test, he was thrilled. I honestly think he was happier than I was.

Five years later I started law school.

It takes only one person to believe in a child. One teacher. That's all it took. I wouldn't be who I am, or where I am, without his support. 

Best to everyone here this morning on the MD stoop,
OC

comments.body:
It was during Labor Day when I was told of my mother's terminal cancer diagnosis so many decades ago.  I was in college and this news hit me harder than a fast ball by Nolan Ryan.  

I promised my mother I would come home on weekends to cook, clean, and do laundry for my dad.  It was a difficult promise because of my tense relationship with my dad but I kept it to ease her mind rather than for any comfort to my dad.

I would walk to the local small town butcher shop and get stuff for a stew or pot roast for my dad so he'd have something substantial to eat all week.

The two butchers loved my mother.  They would kibitz back and forth in-between her choosing various cuts of meat.  When I went in there to get some meat, they asked about where my mother was. The butcher shop went silent.  The older man had to turn away because I knew he had tears in his eyes.  After a few moments he asked me what he could get me.  I told him what I was making for my dad.  He left the counter and came back a few moments later with a rather larger than usual white wrapped package.  He said "Everything you need is in here.  I put in the freshest stuff we just got in.  It's the same stuff your sweet mother would ask for."  I said there was no price on the wrapping.  He said it was a gift from him in honor of my mother's friendship with him over the years.  

Each week I returned to get fresh meat yet I was never charged. I left him $20 as a tip every week.  I told him it was a gift from my mother.

comments.name: AReasonableMan
comments.body:
The author may be right that social science needs more public funding, but the piece is unconvincing special pleading. She concedes that industry-funded research may be rigorous and objects only that companies shape the questions. The NSF does this too, through program officers and peer review panels with their own well-documented biases, and a decade of replication failures shows that academic incentives are no guarantee of truth. The choice is not between pure and captured research but between one funder and many, and a plurality of funders is the healthier system.

Commercial research operates under a discipline the academy lacks: a result that doesn't hold up costs money. In my own field, biomedicine, Amgen scientists reported in 2012 that they could reproduce only six of fifty-three landmark preclinical cancer papers, and Bayer found similar rates. Industry researchers' frustration with unreliable academic work is not new. Nor is the academy's tendency to drift from broader public values; social psychologists themselves have documented how their field's political homogeneity distorts what gets studied and what is believed. The academy has never had a monopoly on truth, and the AI companies now hiring social scientists, philosophers and psychologists are more likely to widen the conversation than to narrow it.

articles.title: At Taiwan’s Temples, a Glimpse of What China Could Have Been
articles.byline: Lingling Wei | Photography by Sean Marc Lee for WSJ
articles.summary: Decades of separation have produced two very different religious lives on either side of the Taiwan Strait. In Taipei’s crowded temples, a Chinese-born reporter witnesses what was lost.

comments.body: The two ideologies that have literally killed hundreds of millions of people in human history - socialism/communism and RoP.

comments.name: Anthony Taylor
comments.body: It is good--and necessary--to keep reminding that Xi and the CCP turn everything into an abomination.

comments.name: Stephen Cheng
comments.body: Free flow faith is flourishing in China, behinds closed doors and in secret. This is something embedded in the human DNA’s, something a State, no matter how authoritarian, can ever take away.

comments.name: Barnaby Cooperstein
comments.body:
Three interesting facts to reconcile: People seem happier where religious expression is permitted; wealthy nations are less religious than poor nations;  more people believe in religion than believe in supreme beings. The problem with organized religion is that it gains and uses power to challenge the state. The optimum arrangement appears to be "religion light": Provision for places where there is social contact, rituals, spiritual instruction -- but no clerical hierarchy. Jesus did not prescribe popes, cardinals, archbishops, etc..

Too much religion seems to breed fanaticism and hallucinatory thinking. E.g., "supreme leaders."

comments.name: Fresnel Grey
comments.body:
Thank you. Wonderful and insightful article. Speaking of “Sinicization” of religion, I have a different recollection of that. Perhaps less sinister than what the essay mentions here.

I remember a documentary about early Buddhism in China from decades ago. Gosh, I can’t remember the title. The film traced the gradual transmission of Buddhism across the hinterlands that straddled ancient China and India.

One interesting thematic angle the documentary took was to follow the evolution of the statues that depicted the Buddha. In earlier shrines situated in India, the Buddha’s features depicted his Indian heritage. But by the time the religion arrived in China, the early temples built there now showed the Buddha looking very much like a Chinese man.

That history of temples, spanning a few centuries, traced the gradual adaptation of Buddhism. It’s as if the Buddha got up and trekked across the mountainous border, and by the time he sat down to rest, he had been transformed — Sinified.

comments.name: Loren Aandahl
comments.body: Taiwan and China have evolved into completely different societies. This goes much further back than the Nationalist retreat from the mainland in 1949. Recall that Taiwan was a Japanese colony for 50 years from  1895 to 1945. Taiwan has everything China does not. A democratic government, freedom of religion, of association, of speech, etc.

comments.name: CHING CHANG TSAI
comments.body:
Just across the Taiwan Strait about 126 KM, it is China's Fujian province where most of the Taiwanese ancestors came from. One should visit there and take a closer look before making any conclusion about religions. 

Buddhism, Taoism, Islam, Protestant Christianity and Catholic Christianity are the only large and populous religions legally recognized by the Chinese government. There are many other much smaller religions branches. 

On the other hand, there are millions of non-religious people in China. Of course, most of them still believe in God or Gods, but these God or gods are different from the western definition. And these Chinese just don't go to a physical religious location to pray every weekend.  I would say 99% of the Chinese people believe in being good and doing good things. China as well as Japan probably has the lowest crime rates in the world, I think.

By the way, Chinese probably provide the most travelers in terms of trips to overseas in the world. They know what religion is good and/or not good.

comments.name: KJG
comments.body: I’m 5’2” on a good day and even I have problems with airline seats. I can’t imagine the discomfort taller people have to deal with.  Airlines, please stop packing us in like sardines.  I guarantee behavior will improve.

comments.name: AinBmore
comments.body: I enjoy Tyler’s Tall People videos on Facebook.  They are so full of life and affirming.  Bravo to him.

comments.name: Wordier
comments.body:
My daughter is 6 foot 4 inches tall in bare feet. She’s also intelligent (graduated summa cum laude from the best engineering college in our state). Also well read, insightful, and a musician. But when people first meet her all they can think to ask is….”Do you play basketball?”.
The stereotyping is most annoying. People need to think before they speak. 
Would she ask a short man if they work at Willy Wonka’s chocolate factory? .. Nope. Too nice for that.

comments.name: Renee C.
comments.body: I entered the 7th grade in 1968 being 6' tall. Now 70 and still the same height, I don't even think about it. Married someone shorter as all the tall guys seemed to gravitate to the shorter girls. But the advantage is that my daughters are average height and they didn't have to endure all the name calling I endured growing up.

comments.name: PeterR
comments.body:
My Aunt Muriel was 6' 2" and i vaguely recall she was part of a "Tall Girl's Club" here in NYC in the late 1950s/early 1960s - the point being that tall women could meet tall men. 
She did meet and marry the man who became Uncle George.

comments.name: Liz
comments.body:
Barron Trump, who never socializes and everyone says it’s because he’s too tall and he would stick out in a crowd and be embarrassed, should join this group.  Surely if Barron was on the internet he would be aware of these fun loving guys and gals.
Being normal and having friends is very important in forming healthy relationships with the opposite sex.  These guys seem terrific.  Everybody needs friends!

comments.name: Phinneyfir
comments.body: These tours are a great idea!  I was nearly 6” tall by 7th grade in 1970.  You cannot understand just how unrelentingly cruel both children and adults can be.  The stupid comments never end, even as one grows older.  These groups give tall people a chance to socialize without having to deal with casual abuse.

comments.name: Deborah
comments.body: The average heights you refer to seem more appropriate for the 1960’.  My 6 foot tall father was considered tall in the 50’s, but my 6’2” son in the 80’s was average. His son is 6’7” tall and is slightly above average height.  I wonder what the average height will be when the current generation reaches their majority?  Me…well I would be satisfied just being able to see in the bottom shelf of my upper cupboards without a stool.

Instability among the young is also driving the Democratic Party to the left. 
What may happen in China worries those in power.

comments.name: Vagabond Rambler
comments.body: I always find the term "AI Expertise" to be such an oxymoron, and in so many ways.

comments.name: Kalidan
comments.body:
What does 'AI expertise' mean?  Exactly what competencies should a fresh graduate (of any major) demonstrate in terms of this expertise?  Use ChatGPT (or similar)?  Capacity to employ AI agents, or create them?  Design agentic AI for comprehensive solutions?  Should they have full competence in machine learning, in deep learning?

The notion of AI-competence is obtuse and meaningless.  Replace 'AI competence' with 'computer competence.'  Does that latter inform anyone about requirements for teaching and learning in universities?  What would an instructor in a liberal arts program do to produce AI competence?  Did writing an essay on a McIntosh display 'computer competencies'?

The dullest among us are talking the loudest, they want shape policy, decide what is ethical, and put brakes on those using AI.  That is, without possessing any way of even knowing what LLMs are (or how they are designed or work), never heard of machine learning or deep learning.

AI will replace people in the same way Windows suite replaced stenographers, report-writers, and mid-level managers.  It did not cause extinction of human race because people rapidly learned and adapted.  So will we now.  Young ones will start using AI agents, develop proficiency, escalate their productivity.  Until limits of AI are hit.

Exactly in the way that the workforce is inordinately more skilled and productive today than it was a hundred years ago.

comments.name: Gene
comments.body: China's authoritarian form of government is better positioned than others to respond to this new age of hyper productivity.  They can simply let the new A.I. powered economy thrive and profit but tax them enough to create new work and assign it to the unemployed. Big money politics wouldn't allow such a scheme in the United States.  During the Great Depression we put the unemployed to work in the national parks clearing hiking trails, for instance.

comments.name: Laurie Zucker-Conde
comments.body: It's very expensive to slowly die in the US, and scary. I'm still working for another a year or two and I'm pretty much the home care for a spouse with Parkinson's. We pay for health insurance, Medicare, meds, which always increase. These continuing care communities are primarily for wealthy to upper middle class folks who enter as healthy people in their late 60-70s. On the other end, the people who've got no assets but Social Security are on Medicaid. The majority of people in the US are not well served and are paying for duplication of services in their medical insurance, life insurance, disability insurance, home health care aides. The majority of the population is elderly or tending in that direction. Deporting immigrants also does not serve the aging. Instead of making aging a financial opportunity, a National Health Care plan with tax incentives for retrofitting homes and and voluntary national service supporting home care that reduces or funds college might be a different take versus squeeze the last dollar to make people feel guilty for being sick, aging, or needing care.

comments.name: Gary

comments.name: Richard Reisman

comments.name: GMO
comments.body: At 78, my wife and I are on the fast track to our 80's. The "Death Decade," I call it. But we're lucky so far, no major health issues threatening to return us to dirt. I have a long term care policy that may or may not be helpful. My wife says I'm her long term policy. Yeah, sure... But we'll stay in our home until the body removal folks pick us up and return us to dirt. Could be a little smelly in the end, but we won't mind.

comments.name: M
comments.body:
If I remember correctly, Atul Gawande in Being Mortal noted that “Assisted Living” has no universal standard-anything can call themselves that. It seems to me that this is the same with CCRCs.
The nicest CCRCs (even nonprofit) are prohibitively expensive, even for healthy, young seniors who own their modest home with no mortgage, worked all their lives, have no children and no debt (currently financially comfortable).  
I think it is because of income disparities and the widely varying cost of living across the geographic U.S. If you don’t have an inheritance from successful Silent Generation parents, good luck getting into a place comparable with how you live now!
Thanks for covering this and please continue to do so. The model in the article might be more affordable.

articles.title: Getting Benefits of Retirement Home Care, at Your Own Home

comments.name: Brent
comments.body: Almost all of Route 66 is now interstate highway infested with big rig trucks.  66 may be historic, but if you really want to experience Americana, you gotta get off the interstates and onto the two lane byways.

comments.name: DC Denizen
comments.body: Hooray! Wonderful piece.

comments.name: Edward Jawer
comments.body: Great story! That there are those from other countries with such  interests seems remarkable.

comments.name: Peter
comments.body:
Hi Ken, many thanks for the great article - Katie and I (both parts of the group as you know) enjoyed every mile of the Route 66. And, as Wolfgang already said many times whilst being on the (Mother) road: we really only started to appreciate the tour, all of the great people we met, the scenery and the really inspiring atmosphere left and right when we returned. Now looking back to it we would certainly do it again, maybe slowing down the pace here and there - don't ask for our reply when we dropped off the bikes in LA and the back still aching :).
And yes: we do have many really great biker roads out here (living 50 miles off the Nürburgring, other participants living in Switzerland or in the Black Forest). But that's a different way of riding and it was not what Katie and I (and the rest of the group I assume) were looking for - we don't have something like a Route 66 in Europe that has been of such a historic significance or has similar myths or stories "built" around it. Sure, not all are true and some need a detailed subsumption: but the appeal of the Route 66 to European bikers is similar to (coming from a racing background) the Nürburgring or the Isle of Man TT. You just have to go there once in your biker lifetime if you can! Oh, and by the way: we are looking into a bike trip covering the East of the US, just food for thought :-).Have a good and enjoy riding! Peter

comments.name: Meanwhile, Trump-Epstein
comments.body: I still love my journeys with Tod and Buz and Lincoln, listening to Nelson Riddle.

The more famous the star, the more expensive the room.  A brochure about the hotel mentions that it happens to be haunted, a claim which was affirmed by the receptionist the last time I was there.

comments.name: Rhys Martin
comments.body: Wonderful article! Route 66 is often referred to as a linear vilage and this write-up really highlights the fact that we are all a big family. It's such a great community and remains a trip worth taking after a century of evolution and reinvention. Thank you for sharing the perspective of so many people that hold the road dear.

articles.title: ‘Go Get Your Kicks’: The Europeans Obsessed With a U.S. Highway

comments.name: Mark Lee
comments.body: The ultimate distribution endpoints for physical products like chips are no more secure than distribution endpoints of data. Both the Chinese and the Americans are very well aware of this.

comments.name: FritzHJ
comments.body: Simply changing the name of a company in order to evade sanctions is such an obvious ruse tht Nvidia must have known that's what they were doing.  How can Nvidia get away with it?

comments.name: Tom
comments.body: So a name change puts them beyond the fed's reach? Grand.

comments.name: Auntie Mame Again
comments.body:
Can't put the genie back in the bottle... as if this was not bound to happen... and the Federal Government geniuses who are supposed to be monitoring all this, asleep at the wheel or on vacation per usual.  

Great reporting.    

Have the Chinese retro-engineered the chips so they can make their own yet? 

Best detective story of the moment.  True Crime.  (Maybe should be an NYTimes section in the Magazine?)

comments.name: Erik
comments.body: Terrific reporting on an important subject that does not get sufficient attention. We are left with questions about why the U.S. export control system within Commerce is so leaky. Lack of leadership at the top? Insufficient will or resources? Or is it just too complicated presently to monitor and control the sprawling tech trade networks and their supply chains spread across the globe. It was certainly easier during the 70's and 80's to impose export controls on the Soviet Union (CoCom) before globalization exploded.

comments.name: Nogi Ichida
comments.body:
I can’t really think how you can effectively ban exports of a small device that can be carried in a suitcase. Chinese companies need it to train their frontier models and to compare with their home-developed chips.

I think the real threat is not the smuggling of advanced AI Nvidia chips. It is the strategy the U.S. government has been playing under administrations from both parties. As it goes without saying in the Tao Te Ching, the key levers of state power must be kept hidden from view.

True strategic assets, whether national military capabilities, core technologies, or vital levers of influence, are most effective when kept hidden, as quiet, unseen leverage. No one denies U.S. leadership in AI chips. But by restricting access so aggressively, it also pushes others, especially China, to develop their own systems that no longer need U.S. inputs.

Eventually, that could diminish U.S. leverage. That is the dynamic we are likely to see in the foreseeable future.

comments.name: brownie
comments.body: Excellent report. Please continue investigating the emerging technology cold war. Most people underestimate the severity of this situation: technology, specifically chips, is rapidly becoming the foundation of all global power.

comments.name: Ana Swanson
comments.body: Reporting this story was a journey. As my colleagues and I were looking into another firm accused of smuggling A.I. chips last year, we came across something remarkable: Billions of dollars of Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips were being exported directly from the U.S. by a unit of a Chinese company, Inspur, that had been sanctioned repeatedly for working with the military.

articles.title: How a Blacklisted Chinese Tech Giant Kept Buying America’s Best A.I. Chips
articles.byline: Ana Swanson, Paul Mozur, Tripp Mickle and Keith Bradsher
articles.summary: Washington imposed sanctions on Inspur because of its work with the Chinese military. But the company’s subsidiary kept shipping Nvidia’s best chips to feed China’s leading A.I. firms.

comments.name: Karen
comments.body:
I used to be an active, church-member Christian. The more involved I became in the work of a high-steeple church in a major Protestant denomination, the more I realized that, while the work I was doing was work that in some ways served the principles of Jesus that I embraced, it was also work that required my increasing immersion in political concerns and differences that felt anything but Christ-like. I concluded and still believe that the church is the most human of institutions and often reflects behaviors and convictions that are anathema to the heart of the Gospel of Jesus. 

My own imperfect solution to the dilemma was to leave the church and find other avenues and companions to live out my faith. While I sometimes still miss certain relationships from my church days, I have generally found greater satisfaction and fulfillment with my life as one who tries to follow Jesus’s ways without a church connection than I was able to within the walls of church.

comments.name: Dana Jones
comments.body: The greater question is the legal validity of the "Trust Clause" in 2026. A classic question is whether local UMC Churches are more like franchises than connected vessels. The local Church pays all of its local expenses and gives a percentage of its income to the UMC. So, again, in 2026, does one own what it has not paid for? Is that logical? The UMC's position is that it provides appointed Pastors. Congregations are forced to accept and pay all related cost to that appointment. Even if they don't want the Pastor, the Bishop can make the decision.  The Christian Church is growing in areas where the decisions are local. Is it time for the UMC to stop focusing on bedroom issues and realize that they were only a smoke screen for a much larger legal question, The Trust Clause. I find it interesting the many groups that left to denomination, just dropped the "United" from their name. That may well be instructive to the larger Church body.

comments.name: Elizabeth
comments.body:
We quit attending services several years ago at the local Episcopal Church because the national church had become too political. I don’t like being told what to think politically from the pulpit, and we were not the only people to leave. 

Churches should not be political, and they should certainly not be aligned with any political party. The purpose of the church is to teach the Word of God, and mainstream churches are losing members because they’ve strayed from their proper mission.

comments.name: Michael C
comments.body: The splintering of denominations has been an ongoing phenomenon for a couple of decades now and is likely to continue. It usually boils down to disagreements over two things - acceptance of LGBTQ people and allowing women to be pastors. In my own rural Minnesota town there have been a handful of schisms among the several Lutheran congregations here. Too many people dislike change of any kind and would rather fracture their faith community than open their hearts and minds.

comments.name: vptulsa
comments.body:
It saddens me to see all of the infighting at many denominations, not just the UMC.  For over 30 years, I was proud to be an active member of the UMC because I attended church with people from all backgrounds and origins: I had a church family and I was there several times a week.

Now, like some of the other commenters, I attend church online and read and study at home.  My physical church is the nature habitat I have turned my backyard into: there is peace there.

Many denominations have clauses that state they own the property if the individual church leaves.

comments.name: tyrdofwaitin
comments.body:
As with most conflicts of this kind that I've observed over time, it is very rarely about theology and most often about power and influence.  Since the Dallas church is populated with "the well to do", their financial reliance on the central UMC is minimal, if none.  Their financial freedom permits them to consider extra-doctrinal reforms that suit the congregation but not necessarily the larger church. 

It's not clear to me what the precise sticking points are in this dispute, but given the political cimate in that part of the country, it may well be the Dallas church is seeking freedom from oversight of agendas not yet made public.

comments.name: Justin
comments.body:
Independent churches (non-denominational or otherwise) are a major contributor towards the rise of far right politics. Without a national (or international, in the case of the Anglican and Catholic community) organization to oversee seminary studies, doctrine, and logistics, churches run the risk of promoting preachers who are under-qualified and unvetted. 

Theological study (regardless of what you think about scriptures themselves) is an exercise of scholarship (think the ability to read in multiple languages, understand the historic backdrop of what those texts include, etc.). Independent churches cannot guarantee that level of scholarship.

comments.name: Joyce
comments.body: I left this church because of the twist with politics a few years ago. No thank you, I worship at home, where I know I am welcome. I used to support the good work that this church used to do, but they've become too political.

articles.title: Why the United Methodist Church Is Suing a Thriving Texas Congregation
articles.summary: The fight reflects a larger American phenomenon: Churchgoers increasingly want decisions to be made at the local level, not by a national denomination.

Without that small group of employees in 2001, there would be no PINK brand today!

The deterioration of the brand was NOT due to the employees who worked for the brand.

The deterioration happened due to Les Wexner's involvement with Epstein.  Fantastic talent who grew PINK to what it became were let go, unfortunately, because of Wexner's ties to Epstein. Let's get the facts straight!

comments.name: Linda
comments.body: Very few things stay popular. Instead of revising pink, try something new.

comments.name: Wade
comments.body: My partner primarily wears black clothes, with occasional flourishes of white.  I would welcome a little pink, or green, or even beige every now and then.

comments.name: Liemba
comments.body:
In my view, perhaps the fundamental question to ask is: does anyone actually care about the brand of their loungewear, sleepwear, or underwear, especially when they cannot easily show it off to others?

I understand that many people in society feel pressured, gaslit, or may be shallow enough to pay a lot of money in premium for branded clothing on a regular basis. However, you cannot easily show off the designer labels of your loungewear, sleepwear, or underwear for others to see and envy. Just my two cents.

comments.name: Auntie Mame Again

The most comfortable underwear was was cotton batiste. 

Today I want something that pulls in the stomach and tucks under the rear and thus improves my posture while providing a sleek line under clothing.   Best color nude and some padding in the crotch..  Anyone listening?

comments.name: Meighan Corbett
comments.body: The quality of the VS products and probably Pink too, is abysmal. If the quality were better, more customers would stay.

comments.name: Kimberly S. Johnson
comments.body:
Does your underwear have to be sexy or flirty? Body positivity, more inclusive sizing and gender-neutral clothing have changed the definition of sexy for many women.

That shift has pushed Victoria's Secret to redefine its image, veering away from the supermodel-thin look of the past. For Pink, it's betting that young women will connect with a less sex-forward aesthetic, and instead on one focused fun and flirtation.

articles.title: Can Pink Become Something More Than Victoria’s Secret’s Little Sister?

comments.name: Andrew Porter
comments.body: The doors of Engine Company 205 on Middagh Street in Brooklyn Heights, with its mural depicting the towers with stars for the members lost that day, was moved to the 9/11 Museum. Today, the windows of the new doors reproduce that mural.

comments.name: Fozwort
comments.body: Some folks don't need murals to remember.  I was in DC at our company's legal offices when the towers were hit and then the Pentagon.  They turned us out onto the street and we walked back to the train station for the trip home.  My son was working in Manhattan and had to walk home to Brooklyn in the haze and confusion.  My Mom was on a bus trip in PA near Shanksville.  Nobody could reach my cellphone and we all feared for the worst.  We survived but that day will live forever.

comments.name: Elgin Phelps
comments.body:
My son turned 39 in July. He said his friends and cohort were all emotionally damaged. 
I asked why.
"It started with 9/11, followed by the crash in 2008 where many of my friend's families lost their homes, and then Covid hit."

comments.name: larkspur
comments.body: "Never Forget" seems less about the heroism of service and more about doubling down on racism, hatred, and revenge these days.   Republican wars against Islamic states has defined the 21st C.

comments.name: Etaoin Shrdlu
comments.body: The Post Office on Manor Road has a memorial in stained glass.

comments.name: rm
comments.body: Having lived through that horrific day and the aftermath, I still carry the asbestos scarring in my lungs from the smoke. And more tragically, the loss of friends and co-workers.  So, I do my best now to forget that day, and try to ignore the failure of my country, but cannot ignore the heroes.

comments.name: CM
comments.body: I taught for many years at a public high school on Tinton Ave in the South Bronx. Our building had a bold, bright mural commemorating local people who died on 9/11. It wore away over time and was eventually painted over. While I was somewhat startled to see it go, it is more respectful to remove it entirely rather than allow it to persist as a shadow of itself.

articles.title: See What New York City’s Murals Tell Us About 9/11, 25 Years Later
articles.summary: They commanded us to never forget, even as they faded over time. Or was that the point all along?

comments.name: stephan morrow
comments.body:
The S.I. ferry is enough for me is all I can say. I've seen these other ferries but the 20 min ride to S.I. from South Ferry including going past the Liberty Lady is still tops in my book. Not to mention that the price is right (free). You really feel you're way out on the ocean on it and it's a full navigational experience on the open water. Jus' sayin' (many yrs ago a girlfriend and I went on the ferry at night and hung out at the bow area and while she and I conducted a (white) magic ritual after I had been warned by a bruja that I was in some danger after attending a 'mesa blanca' ceremony (don't ask how I got there) and was warned about going near a car with a blue trunk (looking Italian I guess made them think of nothing less than a visiting mobster - I was a screenplay writer). Anyway, Consuelo and I felt like we were skimming through the universe in a Star Wars scenario - just looked like space so much in the darkness of the harbor night - and we did what we were told to do and I felt much better afterwards. Safer. With real estate prices being so high I don't see that many Botnicas around as I once did - and which where this whole saga had begun. The cherry on top was wandering over to Hong Fat's for a birthday feast (it wasn't a tourist magnet yet). Such a sweet woman - ended up marring a famous actor in Russia (have no idea how that happened. ).
Artistic Director
The Great American Play Series

comments.name: Tmn
comments.body: OMG! what a wonderful way to experience the city and a diversity of what it has to offer. I will put a place holder for my next trip back seeing family in the NYC area and take that adventure with them.

comments.name: Stefanie
comments.body: As a young married couple in the seventies, we discovered an inexpensive way to entertain out of towners!  Take them on the SI ferry round trip at sunset, which passes the Statue of Liberty, and end up in Chinatown or Little Italy for dinner!  I think the ferry was 5 cents then.   We will have to explore all these other rides on my next visit.

comments.name: pjubf
comments.body: Lovely article. I've been enjoying these ferries for the past couple of years--the ride itself plus easier access to exploring neighborhoods, but learned some new things with this read.  Richmond County (iykyk), here I come.

comments.name: Andy Newman
comments.body:
Riding ferries around New York for 13 hours changed my perspective on a city I’ve reported on and called home for nearly 30 years. Water covers roughly a third of the area of New York City; by day’s end, the city’s rivers, bays, inlets, straits, and channels felt less like barriers to cross and more like the connective tissue knitting the city together. 

We covered over 60 miles by boat — one-twelfth the distance to Bermuda! — all on a $15 pass.”

comments.name: t-bo
comments.body: The ferries are a great way to get around the borough coasts. Are nearby venues using this in social media promotions?

articles.title: 13 Hours, 5 Boroughs, Lots of Boats: Cruising New York City by Ferry
articles.summary: We spent a day bouncing around the city on the expanded NYC Ferry system — making stops at beaches, festivals, beloved bars and more — for just $15.

comments.name: William
comments.body: Does the feeling of superiority contribute to social class or does social class feed the feelings of superiority. Perhaps some of both. Until more recently than we care to acknowledge, the southern United States was a society created from visions of past glory and class based upon feelings of superiority in the face of relative poverty. It was and to some extent remains a post-feudal society where perceptions of nobility and honor are the coin of the realm. There is no wrath like a noble scorned. The South will rise again and make America great again are related and represent retrograde visions of ways of life that never existed.

comments.name: SH
comments.body: I remember visiting a plantation museum in Virginia. The tour guide raved on and on about the owners "gardens", that had received massive funding to restore. Inside his mansion were the owners "important things" china, artwork, and other remnants of former glory days. Not much mention of the slaves whose work enabled the owners riches. In fact, one "replica" of a slave cabin and not much discussion of the folks enslaved here.  As I took a walking path to a nearby waters edge. I thought to myself, here was the place where humans were "sold down the river".  I pledged to never visit another " plantation" again.

articles.title: Piercing the Delusions of a ‘Humane’ Plantation
articles.summary: In “Tower Hill,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning scholar Alan Taylor pulls apart the twisted logic of a Virginia slave owner and his descendants.

comments.name: Marge Keller
comments.body:
“It was actually very difficult to be worthy of a dog.”

I recall another quote from someone who had said "My dog makes me want to be a better person."

 I firmly believe adopting any creature, i.e., dog or cat or anything else, immediately transforms every heart into ever evolving and deepening love.

I'm always afraid to read books like this one because I know I will be crying a lot throughout the reading.  But I believe this book is worth taking the plunge.  Thanks for the review.

articles.title: The Dog Isn’t the Only One Rescued in This Memoir
articles.summary: In “Living With Freddie,” Anna Heyward recalls the pet who taught her “to be human.”

comments.name: Vjosa Isai
comments.body:
President Trump has repeatedly blamed Canadian trade policies for harming American farmers, prompting me to investigate how his punitive 50 percent tariffs are affecting agricultural towns on this side of the border. 

Driving through central Alberta, I found close-knit communities where farmers and local business owners are bracing for the fallout of the tariffs to ripple through their towns. Many hope that the financial pressure on honey producers will encourage other Canadians to buy local.

articles.title: A Bad Year for Bees Gets Worse as Trump’s Tariffs Hit Canada’s Honey Belt
articles.summary: Alberta produces 40 percent of Canada’s honey. This year, rain and President Trump’s trade war have combined to threaten the industry.
